The other morning I watched a squirrel attempt something truly impossible. It had found a whole peanut in its shell, far too large to carry in its mouth, and stood at the base of a tree holding it between its paws, clearly facing an existential crisis. Every time it tried to climb, the peanut would slip. Every time it set the peanut down, it rolled away. The squirrel would scurry after it, retrieve it, and begin again.

I sat there with my coffee, increasingly invested. This had become a story. Would the squirrel succeed? Would it give up? Would it choose violence against the peanut?

After what felt like fifteen minutes of pure, uncut determination, the squirrel did something I didn't expect. It buried the peanut right there at the base of the tree, covered it with leaves, and scampered off empty-handed into the branches. Gone. Just like that.

I sat with my coffee growing cold, feeling strangely moved. The squirrel had accepted its limitations. It had chosen a smaller goal. It had moved on.

Later that day, I found myself thinking about the peanut when I should have been answering emails. About how sometimes the most intelligent thing isn't persistence but pivoting. About how the squirrel probably went and found a smaller peanut, or an acorn, or whatever squirrels eat when they decide to be reasonable.

We talk so much about grit and refusing to quit, and maybe that's important. But there's also something to be said for standing at the base of your tree, holding something too big, and quietly deciding to bury it and try again tomorrow. The squirrel understood something I keep having to relearn: the goal was never the peanut. The goal was getting up the tree.

I hope the squirrel is doing well. I think about it more than I'd admit.
